title: GHA Simulation #4 — Integrity & Judgment
description: A fresh general-workplace set with more emphasis on integrity, confidentiality, quality, policy, and judgment under pressure.

metadata.notes: Original practice content inspired by publicly reported GHA formats. Not official Google questions.

sections.name: Work Style — Agreement Scale
sections.instructions: Choose the response that best reflects how you generally behave at work.

questions.text: I tend to start implementing before I have clearly defined the problem.
I think about edge cases when they could materially change the outcome.
I often assume others have the same background context that I do.
I consider a task finished once the main path works, even if uncommon edge cases remain.
I sometimes avoid making a decision because I do not want to be responsible if it turns out poorly.
I prefer to keep updates brief even when missing context could create confusion.
A rule can be ignored if everyone involved informally agrees it is unnecessary.
I look for evidence that could challenge my first hypothesis.
I summarize decisions so that people know what will happen next.
I consider how my decisions affect the final outcome, not only my assigned deliverable.
I plan my work so that predictable interruptions do not repeatedly cause missed commitments.
I would disclose a mistake that benefited me, even if it was unlikely to be discovered.
When I identify an important risk, I make sure it is visible to the right people.
Once I complete my assigned part, I rarely check whether the broader outcome succeeded.
I can remain effective even when a project changes direction more than once.
I find it difficult to proceed when the decision-maker has not specified exactly what success looks like.
I change my approach when credible feedback reveals a weakness.
I often need external pressure before I finish routine but important work.
I can commit to a reasonable path while remaining open to changing it later.
I prefer familiar solutions even when the problem has important differences from past cases.
I try to understand disagreement before assuming someone is being difficult.
I can support a team decision even when another option was my personal preference.
Unexpected requests often cause me to lose track of earlier commitments.
If nobody is harmed, small conflicts of interest do not always need to be disclosed.
I am uncomfortable starting until most important details are fully specified.
I seek input from people who will be affected by a decision when their perspective could improve it.
I usually need a concrete failure before I reconsider a familiar approach.
When time is short, I tend to rely on people whose opinions I already know.
I escalate when a deadline would otherwise force an unacceptable quality or safety tradeoff.
I prefer roles where priorities remain stable for long periods.

sections.name: Workplace Judgment
sections.instructions: For each scenario, choose the action you would be MOST likely to take and the action you would be LEAST likely to take.

questions.scenario: A teammate tells you they feel excluded from decisions that affect their work.

actions.text: Ask for specific examples, understand the impact, and adjust the decision process where appropriate.
Explain that decisions need to stay efficient and not everyone can be involved.
Invite them to every meeting regardless of relevance.
Tell them to raise it with their manager instead.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You have two reasonable solutions: one is faster now, the other reduces likely future maintenance.

actions.text: Compare the near-term need, future cost, reversibility, and evidence before choosing.
Always choose the faster solution.
Always choose the more maintainable solution.
Delay until you can build both.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A report contains a mistake that makes your team's results look slightly better.

actions.text: Correct the mistake and notify the relevant people if they may have relied on the earlier result.
Leave it because the difference is small.
Correct it silently in the next version.
Wait to see whether anyone notices.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You are asked to mentor a colleague while your own workload is high.

actions.text: Agree on a manageable form of support and communicate any capacity tradeoff.
Decline because mentoring is not part of your delivery goals.
Accept fully and let your own deadlines slip.
Give them documents and avoid further interaction.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A cross-functional partner uses terminology your team finds confusing.

actions.text: Agree on shared definitions and confirm understanding before important decisions.
Keep using your team's terminology and expect them to adapt.
Avoid involving the partner in technical discussions.
Let the misunderstanding continue unless it causes a problem.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You have a promising idea but little evidence that it will work.

actions.text: Design a small, low-cost test to learn whether the idea is worth pursuing.
Build the full solution so the idea gets a fair chance.
Drop the idea because the evidence is weak.
Present it as proven so you can get support.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A colleague asks you to approve work you have not had time to review.

actions.text: Be clear that you cannot responsibly approve it yet and find the fastest appropriate review path.
Approve it because you trust the colleague.
Approve it with a note that you did not review it.
Ignore the request until the deadline passes.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: Your team is missing a deadline because another group changed a requirement late.

actions.text: Explain the impact factually, re-plan with the new requirement, and avoid assigning blame unnecessarily.
Emphasize that the delay is entirely the other group's fault.
Ignore the new requirement and deliver the original scope.
Stop work until leadership resolves responsibility.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You are unsure whether information in a document is allowed to be shared externally.

actions.text: Check the classification or ask the appropriate owner before sharing.
Share it if it does not look sensitive.
Remove obvious confidential sections and share the rest.
Ask the external recipient to keep it private.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A teammate proposes an approach you initially dislike, but their data supports it.

actions.text: Update your view based on the evidence and help strengthen the chosen approach.
Continue supporting your original idea because you have more experience.
Agree publicly but continue implementing your own plan.
Ask a senior person to settle the disagreement.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A new urgent request arrives while your current task is also high priority.

actions.text: Clarify relative priority and impact, then communicate what will move or slip.
Work on both at once without changing expectations.
Ignore the new request because your current work came first.
Switch immediately and tell the current stakeholder later.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You spot an opportunity to improve a process outside your immediate team.

actions.text: Validate the problem with affected people and propose an improvement through the appropriate channel.
Ignore it because it belongs to another team.
Change the process yourself without consulting the owners.
Complain informally but take no action.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A meeting decision is based on data you know is several months old.

actions.text: Point out the age of the data and assess whether newer information could materially change the decision.
Stay quiet because the data was provided by another team.
Reject the decision entirely without checking whether the old data is still valid.
Use the data but avoid mentioning its age.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A peer repeatedly interrupts another teammate in discussions.

actions.text: Intervene constructively so the teammate can finish and reinforce balanced discussion norms.
Do nothing because the interrupted teammate can speak up for themselves.
Interrupt the peer back to make the point.
Complain privately after the meeting but do not address the pattern.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You are asked for an estimate on a task you have never done before.

actions.text: Break down the work, identify uncertainty, use analogous data where possible, and communicate a range or assumptions.
Give a precise estimate so planning can continue.
Refuse to estimate until you have completed similar work.
Copy the estimate from a superficially similar task.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored
